questions.stem: In a classroom demonstration, two iron energy levels are separated by 4.25e-21 J; at 307 K compute the Boltzmann population ratio of the upper to the lower level.

options.misconception: Used a positive exponent and exceeded one
Reported the exponent itself rather than its exponential
Inserted an extra factor of two in the denominator
Correct application of the principle

questions.explanation: The Boltzmann distribution gives the upper-to-lower population ratio as exp of minus delta E over kT. With separation 4.2e-21 J, k equal to 1.380649e-23, and 307 K the ratio is 0.3670; since the upper level lies higher, fewer molecules occupy it at thermal equilibrium.
questions.hint: N_upper/N_lower = exp(-delta E / kT).

questions.subject: THERMODYNAMICS
questions.learningObjective: Apply Mean Translational Kinetic Energy principles to solve a quantitative thermodynamics problem.
questions.stem: In a benchtop measurement, at 256 K, calculate the mean translational kinetic energy of an iron gas molecule using Boltzmann's constant 1.380649 times ten to the minus 23 J per K.

options.misconception: Used three kT instead of three halves kT
Omitted the three translational degrees of freedom
Correct application of the principle
Used the gas constant instead of the Boltzmann constant

questions.explanation: Each translational degree of freedom contributes half of kT, and there are three, so the mean translational kinetic energy is three halves kT. With 256 K and k equal to 1.380649e-23 the result is 5.30e-21 J; note this is per molecule, which is why Boltzmann's constant rather than R appears.
questions.hint: Average translational KE = (3/2) kT per molecule.

questions.subject: THERMODYNAMICS
questions.learningObjective: Apply van der Waals Pressure principles to solve a quantitative thermodynamics problem.
questions.stem: In a classroom demonstration, for 2.1 mol of neon in 3.8 L at 428 K, use the van der Waals equation with a 3.21 and b 0.024 and R 0.08314 L bar per mol K to find the pressure in bar.

options.misconception: Used the ideal gas law and ignored both corrections
Applied only the excluded-volume attraction and omitted the b correction
Correct application of the principle
Applied only the volume correction and omitted the attraction term

questions.explanation: The van der Waals equation corrects the ideal law for molecular attraction and finite size: P equals nRT over (V minus nb) minus a n squared over V squared. With the given constants and 2.1 mol at 428 K, the pressure is 18.95 bar; the attraction lowers pressure while excluded volume raises it.
questions.hint: P = nRT/(V - nb) - a(n/V)^2 using van der Waals constants.

questions.subject: THERMODYNAMICS
questions.learningObjective: Apply Compressibility Factor principles to solve a quantitative thermodynamics problem.
questions.stem: In a classroom demonstration, a xenon sample has pressure 26 atm, volume 1.78 L, 1.5 mol, and temperature 431 K; compute its compressibility factor Z using R 0.082057.

options.misconception: Shifted the temperature before computing Z
Inverted the compressibility-factor ratio
Used the energy-based gas constant in a L atm expression
Correct application of the principle

questions.explanation: The compressibility factor is Z equals PV over nRT, measuring deviation from ideality; Z equals one for an ideal gas. With pressure 26 atm, volume 1.78 L, 1.5 mol, and 431 K the value is 0.872; values below one indicate net attractive interactions.
questions.hint: Z = PV/(nRT) with R consistent with the pressure and volume units.

questions.subject: THERMODYNAMICS
questions.learningObjective: Apply Joule-Thomson Coefficient principles to solve a quantitative thermodynamics problem.
questions.stem: In a laboratory check, for a helium gas modelled with van der Waals constants a 2.28 and b 0.036, molar heat capacity 44 J per mol K, and temperature 426 K, estimate the Joule-Thomson coefficient in K per bar using R 0.08314.

options.misconception: Reversed the sign of the coefficient
Correct application of the principle
Omitted the heat-capacity divisor
Used only half the attraction term

questions.explanation: For a van der Waals gas the Joule-Thomson coefficient is approximately (1/Cp) times (2a over RT minus b). Substituting a 2.28, b 0.036, Cp 44, and 426 K gives 0.0021 K per bar; a positive value means throttling cools the gas, which is exploited in liquefaction.
questions.hint: Mu_JT ~ (1/Cp)(2a/(RT) - b) for a van der Waals gas.

questions.stem: for neon at a molar volume of 195 cubic cm per mol the second virial coefficient is -34 cubic cm per mol; using the truncated virial equation Z = 1 + B/Vm, find the compressibility factor.

options.misconception: Correct application of the principle
Used a negative sign before the virial term
Multiplied by the molar volume instead of dividing
Reported the virial correction alone instead of one plus it

questions.explanation: The truncated virial equation expresses the compressibility factor as one plus the second virial coefficient divided by molar volume, Z equals 1 plus B over Vm. With B -34 and Vm 195 cubic cm per mol the result is 0.8256; the sign of B reflects whether attractions or repulsions dominate.
questions.hint: Z = 1 + B/V_m using the truncated virial expansion.

questions.subject: THERMODYNAMICS
questions.learningObjective: Apply Fugacity principles to solve a quantitative thermodynamics problem.
questions.stem: In a benchtop measurement, an argon gas at 49 bar has a fugacity coefficient of 0.864. Compute its fugacity in bar.

options.misconception: Correct application of the principle
Used one minus the coefficient times pressure
Divided pressure by the fugacity coefficient
Added the coefficient to the pressure

questions.explanation: Fugacity is the effective pressure that replaces pressure in thermodynamic expressions for real gases, defined as the fugacity coefficient times the true pressure, f equals phi P. With coefficient 0.864 and pressure 49 bar the fugacity is 42.34 bar; an ideal gas has phi equal to one so f equals P.
questions.hint: Fugacity f = phi P, where phi is the fugacity coefficient.
